section.title: Overview
section.p: Three numbers in the emulator's SWI chunk are allocated but are not implemented. They are recorded here so that a host implementation knows not to expect them, and so that nobody reuses a number for something else and then finds a guest built against the original meaning.
None of the three is intercepted. A guest issuing one of them reaches RISC OS, which reports an unknown SWI, exactly as it would for any other unallocated number.

value-table.value: Shutdown. Inherited from ArcEm, where it stopped the emulator from inside the emulated machine. Not implemented here
Debug. Inherited from ArcEm, where it wrote diagnostics to the emulator's own output. Not implemented here
Reserved. Never allocated a meaning in either emulator, and never used

subsection.title: Shutdown
subsection.p: &hex;56AC0 stopped the emulator when called from inside the emulated machine. RPCEmu reaches the same end differently and without a SWI of its own: the RISC OS Switcher is patched at run time to advertise that the machine supports power control, so the desktop's Shutdown finishes by calling with the documented request to power the machine off. The emulator recognises that and closes itself. Any other is a genuine reset and is passed through untouched.

The effect is that shutting the machine down from the desktop closes the emulator, with nothing needed inside the machine to arrange it. A host implementation wanting the same behaviour should follow the same route rather than implement this SWI.

subsection.title: Debug
subsection.p: &hex;56AC2 wrote diagnostics from the emulated machine to the emulator's output. RPCEmu has its own debugging facilities which do not need the guest's cooperation - a debugger driven over a socket, exception trapping, SWI tracing and logging watchpoints - so nothing has required this.

subsection.title: Reusing them
subsection.p: Both numbers should be treated as spent rather than free. Guest software built for ArcEm may still issue them, and a number given a new meaning here would be called with the old one's registers by anything that had not been rebuilt. A new interface should take a new number in the chunk instead; &hex;56AC6 onwards are unused, as is everything between &hex;56AC6 and &hex;56AD0 aside from the clipboard's number itself.
